subject: Mathematics
title: Vikram's Tile Shop: Exploring Shapes
hook: Vikram's family owns a tile shop. Learn about shapes, angles, and symmetry through colorful patterns!

characters.name: Vikram
characters.role: boy learning about shapes in his family's tile shop

characters.name: Papa
characters.role: tile shop owner who knows shapes and patterns

characters.name: Divya
characters.role: Vikram's classmate who loves art and design

slides.title: Geometry
slides.storyContext: Vikram helps arrange tiles in his father's shop and discovers beautiful shapes and patterns.

slides.title: The Tile Shop Mystery
slides.storyContext: Papa says, 'Vikram, these tiles aren't just square! Look—some are triangles, some are circles. And these patterns! See the symmetry?' Divya visits and says, 'I love the hexagon tiles! They fit perfectly together.' Vikram wonders: 'How do all these shapes fit together? What makes them special?'

slides.title: Vikram Sorts the Tiles
slides.storyContext: Papa asks Vikram to organize new tiles by shape. 'Put all the pointy ones here, the smooth round ones there,' he says. Vikram moves slowly, touching each tile, noticing differences. Some tiles feel sharp at the corners, others smooth all around. He stacks them by category.

points.text: Different shapes have different looks and feels.
Sorting by shape helps us understand what makes each special.

slides.title: 2D Shapes: Sides and Vertices
slides.storyContext: Papa shows Vikram different flat tiles and they count the corners (vertices) and edges (sides).

points.label: Triangle
points.text: 3 sides, 3 corners (vertices)

points.label: Square
points.text: 4 equal sides, 4 right angles, 4 corners

points.label: Rectangle
points.text: 4 sides (opposite sides equal), 4 right angles, 4 corners

points.label: Circle
points.text: No sides, no corners, perfectly round

example.problem: Papa shows a hexagon tile. How many sides and corners does it have?
example.solution: A hexagon has 6 sides and 6 corners.

slides.inSimpleWords: Shapes are made of straight sides and pointy corners, except circles which are smooth and round.

slides.title: Counting Sides: Triangles vs Squares
slides.storyContext: Vikram picks up a triangular tile and a square tile. Papa asks him to count and compare.

example.problem: A triangle has 3 sides. A square has 4 sides. How many more sides does a square have?
example.solution: 4 - 3 = 1. A square has 1 more side than a triangle.

points.text: Triangle: 3 sides, 3 corners
Square: 4 sides, 4 corners
More sides = shape gets more corners too

slides.title: Right Angles and Corners
slides.storyContext: Vikram learns that some corners in shapes are special. Papa says, 'These tiles have four right angles. See? They fit perfectly into the wall!'

points.label: Right angle (90°)
points.text: a perfect corner, like the corner of a book or the edge of a square

points.label: Squares and rectangles
points.text: have four right angles

points.label: Triangles
points.text: may have one, or no right angles

points.label: Check with a square tool
points.text: A small square corner can test if angles are right

example.problem: Does a triangle always have a right angle?
example.solution: No. Some triangles have one right angle, some have none. The sum of all angles in a triangle is 180°.

slides.inSimpleWords: A right angle is a corner that is exactly square, like the corner of a cardboard box.

slides.title: Divya's Corner Test
slides.storyContext: Divya brings a small cardboard square corner from art class. She tests tiles with it. 'This rectangle fits perfectly—four right angles!' she says. She tries it on a triangle tile. 'Only one corner is right.' She tries on a circle. 'No corners at all!'

points.text: Different shapes have different numbers of right angles.
We can test angles using a simple square tool.

slides.title: Line Symmetry: Mirror Images
slides.storyContext: Divya draws a line down the middle of a tile and says, 'Look! If I fold here, both sides match perfectly. That's symmetry!'

points.label: Symmetry
points.text: when both sides of a line are exactly the same

points.label: Line of symmetry
points.text: the imaginary line where you fold

points.label: Examples
points.text: square has 4 lines, rectangle has 2, triangle may have 1 or 0

example.problem: How many lines of symmetry does a square have? A triangle?
example.solution: Square: 4 lines. Triangle: 1 line (only if it's isosceles), 0 lines (if it's scalene).

slides.inSimpleWords: A shape has symmetry if you can fold it and both sides match exactly.

slides.title: Finding Symmetry in Tiles
slides.storyContext: Vikram folds paper copies of different tiles to find their lines of symmetry.

example.problem: Fold a square tile in half. Do both halves match? Now fold it corner-to-corner. Do they match? How many ways can you fold a square so both sides match?
example.solution: A square matches when folded 4 ways: vertically, horizontally, and diagonally (twice). A square has 4 lines of symmetry.

points.text: Squares have 4 lines of symmetry.
Rectangles have 2 lines of symmetry.
Some triangles have 1, some have none.

slides.title: 3D Shapes: Cubes and Cuboids
slides.storyContext: Papa pulls out a tile display box (a cube). 'This is a 3D shape! It has faces (the flat sides), edges (the lines where faces meet), and vertices (the corners).'

points.label: Cube
points.text: 6 square faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices (vertices are called corners in everyday language)

points.label: Cuboid (rectangular box)
points.text: 6 rectangular faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices

points.label: Sphere (ball)
points.text: no faces, no edges, no vertices. Perfectly round in all directions

example.problem: How many faces, edges, and vertices does a cube have?
example.solution: Cube: 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices.

slides.inSimpleWords: 3D shapes have flat faces, lines where faces meet (edges), and pointy corners (vertices).

slides.title: Vikram Builds with 3D Shapes
slides.storyContext: Papa gives Vikram wooden blocks—cubes and cuboids. Vikram stacks them and touches the edges and corners. 'Each corner is like where three walls meet in a room!' he discovers. Papa smiles and corrects: 'That corner is called a vertex.'

points.text: 3D shapes are solid and take up space.
We can count faces, edges, and vertices on 3D shapes.

slides.title: Counting Parts of a Cuboid
slides.storyContext: Vikram's tile display box is a cuboid. He carefully traces and counts each part.

example.problem: Vikram's tile box is shaped like a cuboid (rectangular prism). Count its faces, edges, and vertices.
example.solution: Cuboid: 6 faces (rectangles on all sides), 12 edges (lines where two faces meet), 8 vertices (corners where three faces meet).

points.text: Opposite faces are equal in a cuboid.
Every edge connects two vertices.
Every vertex is where three edges meet.

slides.title: Patterns and Tiling
slides.storyContext: Vikram arranges small tiles into a pattern. Some tiles repeat in rows. Some fit together with no gaps (like hexagons!). Divya says, 'This is tessellation—the shapes tile perfectly!'

points.label: Repeating pattern
points.text: Shapes follow a rule. Example: square, triangle, square, triangle...

points.label: Tessellation
points.text: Shapes fit together with no gaps or overlaps

points.label: Examples
points.text: Squares, rectangles, and hexagons tessellate. Circles don't (they leave gaps)

example.problem: If you tile a floor with only hexagons, will there be gaps?
example.solution: No. Hexagons tessellate perfectly—they fit together with no gaps.

slides.inSimpleWords: Some shapes fit together perfectly to cover a floor with no spaces. Others leave gaps.

slides.title: Designing Vikram's Floor
slides.storyContext: Vikram and Papa plan a new tile floor for the shop entrance. 'We need a pattern that looks beautiful and fits perfectly,' Papa says. Vikram sketches squares and triangles arranged in rows. 'Will they tessellate?' Vikram wonders aloud.

points.text: Designers choose shapes that tessellate well.
Patterns can follow rules like: repeat every 4 tiles, alternate colors, etc.

slides.title: Designing a Tile Pattern
slides.storyContext: Vikram designs a new floor pattern. He uses squares and triangles. Each square has a triangle on top and bottom. How many triangles does he need for 10 squares?

example.problem: Pattern: 1 square needs 2 triangles (one on top, one on bottom). For 10 squares, how many triangles?
example.solution: 10 × 2 = 20 triangles needed.

slides.title: A Hexagon Discovery
slides.storyContext: Divya brings a picture of a honeycomb to the tile shop. 'Look! Bees make perfect hexagons!' Vikram is amazed. Papa explains: 'Hexagons are nature's favorite shape for fitting perfectly. They appear in honeycombs, flower petals, and soccer balls!'

points.text: Hexagons appear in nature and are efficient shapes.
Six-sided shapes fit together without gaps.

slides.title: Why Shapes Matter in Real Life
slides.storyContext: Papa shows Vikram how shapes are everywhere in the tile shop and beyond.

points.label: Architecture
points.text: Buildings use rectangles and triangles for strength and beauty.

points.label: Nature
points.text: Flowers, snowflakes, and honeycombs have perfect symmetry.

points.label: Tiles and patterns
points.text: Shapes tessellate to cover floors and walls without waste.

points.label: Design
points.text: Artists and engineers use symmetry and shapes to create pleasing designs.

slides.inSimpleWords: Understanding shapes helps us build things, appreciate nature, and create beautiful designs.

points.text: Shapes are the foundation of geometry and design.

slides.title: Your Turn: Shape Detective
slides.storyContext: Look at these 2D shapes: A—triangle with all sides equal, B—rectangle, C—circle. (a) Which have right angles? (b) Which have lines of symmetry? (c) If you arrange B in a row, do they tessellate?

example.problem: (a) Which shapes have right angles? (b) How many lines of symmetry does each? (c) Do rectangles tessellate?
example.solution: (a) Rectangle (B) and circle are special; triangle depends on type. (b) Triangle: 1 (or 0), Rectangle: 2, Circle: infinite. (c) Yes, rectangles tessellate perfectly.

image.alt: Your Turn: Shape Detective — Geometry

slides.title: Challenge: Design Your Own Tessellation
slides.storyContext: Vikram is challenged to design a floor pattern using only one type of shape that tessellates perfectly.

example.problem: Choose ONE shape (square, rectangle, or hexagon) and design a pattern that covers a 4×4 grid with no gaps or overlaps. Can you color alternating shapes in two colors?
example.solution: If using squares: arrange in a 4×4 grid (16 squares total). Color alternating squares red and blue like a checkerboard. All gaps are filled, no overlaps. Pattern is balanced and pretty.

points.text: Squares, rectangles, and hexagons all tessellate.
Tessellations can be colored to create patterns.

slides.title: Shapes in Architecture
slides.storyContext: Divya brings pictures of famous buildings: the Taj Mahal (domes and symmetry), temples (triangular roofs), modern offices (rectangles and glass cubes). Vikram realizes: 'All buildings are made of shapes!' Papa nods. 'Architects use shapes to make buildings strong and beautiful.'

points.text: Real buildings use geometry to stand strong.
Symmetry appears in famous architecture worldwide.

slides.title: Shapes in Nature
slides.storyContext: Vikram finds shapes in nature: spider web hexagons, snowflake symmetry, sunflower spiral seeds, honeycomb perfection. 'Nature uses geometry too!' he exclaims. Papa smiles. 'Nature invented geometry millions of years before humans. Every shape has a purpose—efficient, strong, and beautiful.'

points.text: Nature uses perfect geometry for efficiency and beauty.
Shapes appear everywhere in the natural world.

slides.title: Angles in Everyday Objects
slides.storyContext: Vikram finds right angles in the tile shop and beyond.

example.problem: Look around: door frame (4 right angles), book corner (4 right angles), picture frame (4 right angles), pencil point (acute angle), open door (variable angles). How many right angles can you count in this room?
example.solution: Corners of windows, doors, tiles, shelves, tables all have right angles. Most human-made objects use right angles for stability and practicality. Acute angles (less than 90°) are used in roofs and arrows for efficiency.

points.text: Right angles appear everywhere in human design.
Different angles serve different purposes.

slides.title: Vikram Becomes a Tile Master
slides.storyContext: By the end of the week, Vikram can identify shapes, count sides and corners, find lines of symmetry, and design patterns. Papa is proud. 'You've learned geometry through tiles,' he says. Vikram grins: 'Now I see shapes everywhere!'

points.text: Vikram mastered 2D and 3D shapes, angles, symmetry, and tessellation.
Understanding shapes makes the world more interesting.

slides.title: Transformations - Moving Shapes
slides.storyContext: Divya shows Vikram three ways to move shapes: slide, flip, turn.

points.label: Translation (Slide)
points.text: Move a shape without rotating or flipping. A square slides across the floor stays a square.

points.label: Reflection (Flip)
points.text: Mirror a shape across a line. A triangle flipped looks like its mirror image.

points.label: Rotation (Turn)
points.text: Spin a shape around a point. A square rotated 45° becomes a diamond-looking shape.

slides.inSimpleWords: Shapes can slide, flip, and turn but remain the same shape—just in different positions.

points.text: Transformations help us create patterns and designs.

slides.title: Shapes Around You
slides.storyContext: Vikram realizes geometry isn't just in the tile shop. It's in sports (soccer ball spheres), clothing (symmetrical designs), food (circular pizzas, triangular chips), games (dice cubes), and art. 'Every part of the world uses shapes,' he tells Divya. 'We just need to learn to see them.'

points.text: Geometry is everywhere in daily life.
Learning geometry helps you see the world more deeply.
2D shapes are flat: triangles (3 sides), squares/rectangles (4 sides), circles (no sides)
Squares and rectangles have four right angles (90° corners)
Symmetry means a shape's two sides match when folded
3D shapes have faces (flat sides), edges (lines), and vertices (corners)
Cubes and cuboids are common 3D shapes in real life (boxes, dice)
Some shapes tessellate (fit together perfectly) like squares and hexagons

image.alt: What We Learned Today — Geometry

subject: Science
title: Asha's Garden Discovery
hook: Learn how plants grow and what each part does!

slides.title: Plants - Parts and Functions
slides.storyContext: Asha visits her grandpa's garden in Punjab and discovers how plants work.

image.alt: Plants - Parts and Functions — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: In Grandpa's Garden
slides.storyContext: Asha sees vegetables, fruit trees, and flowers. Grandpa asks: 'Do you know why plants have roots, stems, leaves, and flowers?' Asha shakes her head. 'Then let's explore together,' he smiles.

image.alt: In Grandpa's Garden — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: Digging Deep
slides.storyContext: Grandpa and Asha carefully dig near a spinach plant. As they pull the plant gently, long white thread-like parts come out of the soil. 'Those are roots!' Grandpa says excitedly. Asha is amazed. 'There are so many tiny ones!' She touches them—they're wet and cool.

points.text: Roots grow underground and are hidden from sight.
Roots absorb water and stay connected to soil.

slides.title: Roots - The Hidden Workers
slides.storyContext: Grandpa digs gently near a tomato plant and shows Asha the roots hidden below the soil.

points.label: What are roots?
points.text: Roots are parts of the plant that grow underground.

points.label: What do they do?
points.text: Roots drink water and nutrients from the soil.

points.label: They also hold
points.text: Roots keep the plant firmly in the ground so it doesn't fall over.

slides.inSimpleWords: Roots are like a plant's drinking straw and anchor.

image.alt: Roots - The Hidden Workers — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: The Root Test
slides.storyContext: Grandpa shows Asha two plants: one in wet soil, one in dry soil.

example.problem: Grandpa has two identical plants. One is planted in moist soil with strong roots. One is planted in dry soil. After one week, which plant looks healthier?
example.solution: The plant in moist soil is healthier because its roots can absorb water and nutrients. The dry soil plant may wilt because its roots can't find enough water.

points.text: Roots need water in soil to keep plants alive.
Dry soil = weak roots = weak plant.

slides.title: Stems - The Plant's Backbone
slides.storyContext: Asha holds a stick from the mango tree. Grandpa says: 'That's what a stem looks like inside.'

points.label: What is a stem?
points.text: The stem is the main part that grows upward from the ground.

points.label: It carries water
points.text: Water from roots travels up the stem to leaves and flowers.

points.label: It supports
points.text: The stem holds leaves, flowers, and fruits high up in the air.

slides.inSimpleWords: The stem is like the plant's backbone and water pipe.

image.alt: Stems - The Plant's Backbone — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: Tracking Water Through the Stem
slides.storyContext: Grandpa cuts a fresh stem in half. 'See these tiny tubes inside?' He shows Asha the cross-section. 'Water travels up through these like a highway.' He breaks a thin stem and shows her how water trickles out. 'The stem is like thousands of drinking straws bundled together!'

points.text: Stems contain tiny tubes that transport water.
Water travels from roots through the stem to every leaf.

slides.title: Leaves - The Plant's Kitchen
slides.storyContext: Asha touches a mango leaf and looks at the veins running through it. 'What are these lines?' she asks.

points.label: What are leaves?
points.text: Leaves are flat, green parts that grow on the stem.

points.label: They make food
points.text: Leaves use sunlight, water, and air to make food for the plant.

points.label: Veins in leaves
points.text: The lines carry water and food inside the leaf, like roads for nutrients.

slides.inSimpleWords: Leaves are the plant's kitchen where it makes food from sunlight.

image.alt: Leaves - The Plant's Kitchen — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: Why Leaves Are Green
slides.storyContext: Asha asks Grandpa a big question.

example.problem: Why are leaves green and not red or yellow like some flowers?
example.solution: Leaves are green because they contain chlorophyll, a special pigment that captures sunlight. Green is best at absorbing light energy for making food. Some leaves turn red or yellow in autumn when they stop making food.

points.text: Green color = special chemical for capturing sunlight.
Sunlight + water + air in leaves = plant food (glucose).

slides.title: Flowers - The Plant's Gift
slides.storyContext: A bright red chili flower catches Asha's eye. Grandpa grins. 'This flower will become a chili pepper!'

points.label: What are flowers?
points.text: Flowers are beautiful, colorful parts of the plant.

points.label: They make seeds
points.text: After flowers are pollinated, they grow into fruits and seeds.

points.label: They attract
points.text: Bright colors and smells attract bees and butterflies to help make seeds.

slides.inSimpleWords: Flowers are pretty parts that turn into fruits and seeds.

image.alt: Flowers - The Plant's Gift — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: A Bee Visits the Flowers
slides.storyContext: As Asha and Grandpa watch, a honeybee lands on a bright orange marigold. It buzzes and moves from flower to flower. 'What's the bee doing?' Asha wonders. Grandpa explains: 'The bee collects sweet nectar from flowers. But pollen sticks to its body. When it visits the next flower, pollen rubs off. That helps make seeds!' Asha watches in fascination.

points.text: Bees help flowers by moving pollen between them.
This process (pollination) leads to seeds and fruits.

slides.title: Fruits and Seeds - New Plants
slides.storyContext: Grandpa picks a ripe mango. Inside are seeds. 'A new mango tree can grow from this seed,' he says.

points.label: What are fruits?
points.text: Fruits grow from flowers and protect the seeds inside.

points.label: What are seeds?
points.text: Seeds can grow into new plants if they get soil, water, and sunlight.

points.label: From seed to plant
points.text: A tiny seed grows roots, a stem, leaves, then flowers—and the cycle repeats.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fruits protect seeds, and seeds grow into new plants.

image.alt: Fruits and Seeds - New Plants — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: Planting a Mango Seed
slides.storyContext: Grandpa teaches Asha how to grow a new mango tree.

example.problem: Grandpa gives Asha a mango seed from the ripe fruit. To grow it into a plant, what does Asha need to do?
example.solution: Plant the seed in moist soil. Keep it warm. Water regularly. Place in sunlight after it sprouts. After 4-6 weeks, a small shoot will emerge. Asha will see a root growing down and a stem/leaves growing up!

points.text: Seeds need soil, water, warmth, and light to grow.
A seed contains a tiny plant inside just waiting to start.

slides.title: How a Tomato Plant Works
slides.storyContext: Asha watches Grandpa explain a whole tomato plant in the garden.

example.problem: Look at Grandpa's tomato plant. It has roots buried in the soil, a thick green stem, big leaves, yellow flowers, and red tomatoes. How does each part help the plant grow and make tomatoes?
example.solution: Roots drink water from soil. Stem carries water up to leaves and flowers. Leaves use sunlight to make food. Flowers turn into red tomatoes. The tomatoes protect seeds inside that can grow into new plants next year.

image.alt: How a Tomato Plant Works — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: The Plant Cycle Complete
slides.storyContext: Grandpa and Asha sit under the mango tree at sunset. 'This tree has roots underground drinking water. Its stem carries that water to leaves. Leaves catch sunlight and make food. That food helps make flowers. Flowers make seeds in fruits. And those seeds can grow into new trees!' Asha smiles. 'It's a never-ending circle!'

points.text: Plants have a complete life cycle from seed to plant to seed again.
Each part of the plant has a special job in this cycle.

slides.title: What Do You Know?
slides.storyContext: Grandpa gives Asha a riddle: 'I grow under the soil, drink water, and hold the plant tight. What am I?'

example.problem: Grandpa's riddle: 'I grow under the soil, drink water, and hold the plant tight. What am I?' And a second one: 'I am green, flat, and make food for the plant using sunlight. What am I?'
example.solution: First riddle: Roots. Second riddle: Leaves.

image.alt: What Do You Know? — Plants - Parts and Functions

slides.title: Design Your Own Garden
slides.storyContext: Asha is asked to plan a small vegetable garden.

example.problem: Plan a garden with tomatoes, spinach, and radishes. Consider: Where should roots have moist soil? When do flowers appear? When are fruits/seeds ready to harvest?
example.solution: All three need moist soil for roots. Tomato flowers appear in 6-8 weeks (red fruits in 12 weeks). Spinach leaves are harvestable in 4-6 weeks (no flowers needed). Radish roots swell in 4 weeks. Plant tomatoes deep. Water all regularly. Harvest at different times.

points.text: Different plants have different growth timelines.
Understanding plant parts helps us grow food.

slides.title: The Seasons Change
slides.storyContext: Months pass. Asha returns to Grandpa's garden in each season. She watches the mango tree: in spring it blooms with white flowers, in summer it bears green then yellow fruits, in autumn leaves turn yellow, and in winter it rests but roots stay alive underground, ready for spring.

points.text: Plants change with seasons but roots survive year-round.
The plant cycle repeats every year.

slides.title: Photosynthesis - How Plants Make Food
slides.storyContext: Grandpa explains the amazing process that happens inside leaves.

points.label: The magic recipe
points.text: Sunlight + water + air = glucose (food for the plant)

points.label: Chlorophyll
points.text: Green pigment in leaves that captures sunlight energy.

points.label: Why this matters
points.text: Plants make their own food. They don't need to eat like animals. They are self-sufficient!

slides.inSimpleWords: Leaves are like tiny factories that turn sunlight into food using water and air.

points.text: Photosynthesis is the process of making plant food.

slides.title: Why Plants Need Light
slides.storyContext: Asha asks why Grandpa keeps some plants in sunny spots and others in shade.

example.problem: Grandpa has a spinach plant in full sun and one in deep shade. After 4 weeks, which is bigger and greener?
example.solution: The one in full sun is bigger and greener. Why? More sunlight = more photosynthesis = more food made = faster growth and darker green leaves. The shaded plant grows slowly and has pale leaves.

points.text: More light = more photosynthesis = faster growth.
Even low-light plants need SOME light.

slides.title: Pollination Day
slides.storyContext: Asha spends the afternoon watching insects visit flowers. Bees buzz from flower to flower. A butterfly lands on a chili bloom. Grandpa whispers: 'Each visitor carries pollen. Without them, no seeds would form. No seeds means no new plants next year!'

points.text: Pollinators are essential for plant reproduction.
Without insects, many plants couldn't make seeds.

slides.title: Types of Roots
slides.storyContext: Grandpa shows Asha different plants with different root systems.

points.label: Tap roots
points.text: One main thick root going deep (carrot, radish). Good for reaching deep water.

points.label: Fibrous roots
points.text: Many thin roots spreading out (grass, wheat). Good for holding soil.

points.label: Aerial roots
points.text: Roots that grow above ground (ivy, banyan tree). Absorb moisture from air.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different plants have different root shapes for different jobs.

points.text: Root shape matches the plant's needs.

slides.title: Challenge: Grow a Bean in a Jar
slides.storyContext: Grandpa gives Asha a challenge—grow a bean in a clear jar to see all the parts.

example.problem: Place a bean between wet paper towel and clear jar wall. Water daily. Predict: when will you see roots? When will you see leaves? Record what you see each day for 3 weeks.
example.solution: Day 1-2: Bean swells. Day 3-4: roots appear at bottom (white tip). Day 5-7: roots grow longer. Day 7-10: stem grows up. Day 10-14: first leaves unfold. By week 3: small plant with roots, stem, and leaves visible!

points.text: Roots always grow down (gravity), stems always grow up (light).
All plant parts are present in the seed—they just grow bigger.

slides.title: Plants Around Us
slides.storyContext: Asha realizes plants are everywhere: in parks, backyards, forests, fields, even as indoor houseplants. 'Every plant I see now makes sense,' she tells Grandpa. 'I look at any plant and ask: where are its roots? What does its stem do? How do its leaves look? What color are its flowers?' Understanding plant parts helps her appreciate nature's genius.

points.text: Plants are constantly growing and adapting around us.
Knowing plant parts helps you understand the whole world better.

slides.title: Asha Becomes a Gardener
slides.storyContext: By summer, Asha has helped Grandpa grow vegetables, fruit trees, and flowers. She understands each part's job. She knows when to water, when to weed, when to expect flowers. She realizes: 'I'm not just helping plants grow. I'm reading the story that every plant tells through its roots, stems, leaves, and flowers.'

points.text: Understanding plant parts makes you a better gardener.
Every plant tells a story of growth and survival.

slides.title: What Asha Learned
slides.storyContext: As the sun sets, Asha sits under the mango tree with Grandpa, remembering everything.

points.text: Roots drink water and hold the plant in soil.
Stems carry water and hold up leaves and flowers.
Leaves make food from sunlight.
Flowers turn into fruits with seeds.
Seeds grow into new plants.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every part of a plant has an important job to help it grow and make new plants.

image.alt: What Asha Learned — Plants - Parts and Functions

subject: Science
title: Ravi's Healthy Meal Adventure
hook: Discover which foods keep your body strong and healthy!

slides.title: Food and Health
slides.storyContext: Ravi learns why eating right keeps him healthy, strong, and happy.

image.alt: Food and Health — Food and Health

slides.title: Ravi's Energy Drops
slides.storyContext: One morning, Ravi feels tired during cricket practice. His friend plays well, but Ravi can barely run. At school, Doctor Priya checks him. 'Ravi, your body needs the RIGHT food. Let's learn what healthy eating looks like.'

image.alt: Ravi's Energy Drops — Food and Health

slides.title: A Chat with the Doctor
slides.storyContext: Doctor Priya asks Ravi what he had for breakfast. 'Just a glass of juice and some biscuits,' Ravi says. 'No wonder you're tired!' Doctor Priya sits him down. 'Your body is like a machine that needs fuel AND building materials. Juice and biscuits don't have everything you need.'

points.text: Different foods do different jobs in your body.
Breakfast sets you up for the whole day.

slides.title: Food Groups - Building Blocks
slides.storyContext: Doctor Priya shows Ravi a poster of different foods: rice, eggs, fruits, oil, milk.

points.label: We need different foods
points.text: Not one food has everything. We must eat from all groups.

points.label: Five main groups
points.text: Grains (rice, bread), protein (eggs, lentils), vegetables, fruits, dairy (milk, yogurt).

points.label: Each does a job
points.text: Grains give energy. Protein builds muscles. Vegetables and fruits protect your body.

slides.inSimpleWords: Eat foods from all groups to get energy, strong muscles, and good health.

image.alt: Food Groups - Building Blocks — Food and Health

slides.title: The Food Groups In Your Fridge
slides.storyContext: Doctor Priya walks Ravi through what a balanced kitchen looks like.

example.problem: Ravi's fridge has: milk, eggs, rice, carrots, apples, butter, and bread. Which food groups does he have?
example.solution: Milk = dairy. Eggs = protein. Rice = grains. Carrots = vegetables. Apples = fruit. Butter = oils/fats. Bread = grains. He's missing fresh vegetables and could use more variety, but has basic groups covered.

points.text: Most kitchens have foods from most groups.
Balancing meals means choosing from each group.

slides.title: Energy Foods - Grains and Carbs
slides.storyContext: Ravi's mummy makes rotli from wheat flour. Doctor Priya explains why.

points.label: What are they?
points.text: Rice, wheat, bread, pasta—all grains that grow in fields.

points.label: What do they do?
points.text: They give your body energy to run, play, think, and study.

points.label: How much?
points.text: Eat grains at breakfast, lunch, and dinner—your body needs energy all day.

slides.inSimpleWords: Grains are the fuel that keeps you running and playing.

image.alt: Energy Foods - Grains and Carbs — Food and Health

slides.title: Energy for Cricket
slides.storyContext: Doctor Priya explains: 'During cricket, your muscles burn energy. Where does that energy come from? From grains! When you eat rice or bread, your body breaks it down into glucose. Your muscles use glucose to move fast and hit the ball hard.'

points.text: Grains are converted into glucose in your body.
Glucose fuels every movement you make.

slides.title: Body-Building Foods - Protein
slides.storyContext: Doctor Priya asks Ravi: 'Why are your muscles growing strong?' 'I eat eggs and drink milk!' he says proudly.

points.label: What is protein?
points.text: It's in eggs, milk, meat, lentils, beans—foods that build and repair muscles.

points.label: Why do we need it?
points.text: Protein helps your muscles grow big and strong. It repairs your body when you get hurt.

points.label: Where to find it
points.text: Eggs, milk, yogurt, paneer, chicken, fish, lentils, beans.

slides.inSimpleWords: Protein is like building blocks that make your muscles strong.

image.alt: Body-Building Foods - Protein — Food and Health

slides.title: Protein for Growing Bodies
slides.storyContext: Ravi is growing, and his body needs protein to build new muscle.

example.problem: Ravi plays cricket 3 times a week. His muscles get tiny micro-tears during play. What does his body need to repair them and grow stronger?
example.solution: Protein! When Ravi eats protein (eggs, milk, paneer, dal), his body uses it to repair muscle fibers. Over time, muscles grow back stronger. That's why athletes eat lots of protein.

points.text: Muscles need protein to repair and grow.
Daily protein = faster recovery from exercise.

slides.title: Protect & Defend - Fruits and Vegetables
slides.storyContext: Ravi's mummy packs him a lunch box with carrots, spinach, and an apple. 'These keep you healthy,' she says.

points.label: What do they have?
points.text: Vitamins and minerals that protect your body from getting sick.

points.label: Colors mean
points.text: Orange carrots have vitamin A for good eyes. Green spinach has iron for strong blood. Red apples have vitamin C.

points.label: Eat the rainbow
points.text: Different colors = different protections. Eat red, green, yellow, orange fruits and veggies.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fruits and vegetables are like a shield protecting you from illness.

image.alt: Protect & Defend - Fruits and Vegetables — Food and Health

slides.title: Vitamins in the Lunch Box
slides.storyContext: Ravi opens his lunch box and sees colors. 'Orange carrots, green spinach, red tomato, yellow mango,' his mummy says. 'Each color has different vitamins. Together, they keep every part of your body working well—your eyes, bones, blood, immune system, everything!'

points.text: Each color provides different nutrients.
Colorful meals = complete nutrition.

slides.title: Healthy Habits - Water and Cleanliness
slides.storyContext: Doctor Priya shows Ravi something surprising. 'This is as important as food!'

points.label: Drink water
points.text: Your body is mostly water. Drink clean water all day to stay healthy and strong.

points.label: Wash your hands
points.text: Before eating and after playing, wash hands with soap to remove germs.

points.label: Eat clean food
points.text: Wash fruits and vegetables. Cook meat and eggs fully. Store food in clean containers.

slides.inSimpleWords: Clean water and clean hands keep bad germs away from your food.

image.alt: Healthy Habits - Water and Cleanliness — Food and Health

slides.title: The Power of Water
slides.storyContext: Doctor Priya teaches Ravi why water is essential.

example.problem: Ravi plays cricket for 2 hours under the sun. He doesn't drink water during the game. By the end, he feels dizzy and tired. Why?
example.solution: He lost water through sweat. His body couldn't cool itself properly. His muscles didn't work well without water. Lesson: drink water before, during, and after exercise. Aim for 6-8 glasses daily, more on hot days and after sports.

points.text: Water helps your body stay cool through sweating.
Water carries nutrients to cells and removes waste.
Dehydration = fatigue, dizziness, poor performance.

slides.title: Ravi's Perfect Day of Eating
slides.storyContext: With help from Doctor Priya, Ravi plans a healthy day.

example.problem: Ravi wants to eat healthily all day. Plan his breakfast, lunch, snack, and dinner using all food groups.
example.solution: Breakfast: milk with oatmeal and sliced banana (grain, dairy, fruit). Snack: handful of almonds and an orange (protein, fruit). Lunch: rice with lentil dal, spinach curry, and cucumber salad (grain, protein, vegetable). Dinner: rotli with paneer and cooked carrots (grain, protein, vegetable). All day: drink water.

image.alt: Ravi's Perfect Day of Eating — Food and Health

slides.title: Ravi's First Week
slides.storyContext: For one week, Ravi eats balanced meals with all food groups. He drinks lots of water. He washes his hands before eating. By the end of the week, he has more energy during cricket practice. His friends notice: 'You're faster and stronger, Ravi!' He smiles. Good food works!

points.text: Balanced eating shows results in just one week.
Energy, strength, and focus all improve with good nutrition.

slides.title: Spot the Healthy Meal
slides.storyContext: Doctor Priya shows Ravi three lunch boxes. Which one is healthiest?

example.problem: Box A: Only samosas and soda. Box B: Rice, dal, spinach, apple, and water. Box C: Only chocolate and chips. Which lunch box is the healthiest and why?
example.solution: Box B is healthiest. It has grains (rice), protein (dal), vegetables (spinach), fruit (apple), and water. It covers all food groups and has no junk food.

image.alt: Spot the Healthy Meal — Food and Health

slides.title: Design Your Ideal Weekly Menu
slides.storyContext: Ravi is challenged to plan his own healthy week.

example.problem: Plan a 3-day menu (breakfast, lunch, dinner) that includes all food groups, fits Indian meals your family makes, and keeps energy high for sports.
example.solution: Day 1: Breakfast—dosa with sambar (grain, vegetable). Lunch—rice, dal, okra (grain, protein, vegetable). Dinner—roti, paneer bhurji, cucumber (grain, protein, vegetable). Similar variety for Days 2-3 with different grains (wheat, bajra) and veggies. All meals include fruits/milk. All include water.

points.text: Planning meals ahead ensures balanced nutrition.
Variety keeps meals interesting and nutritious.

slides.title: Junk Food Trap
slides.storyContext: Ravi's friend Arjun loves samosas and sodas. Doctor Priya explains why too much junk food is dangerous: 'Junk food has lots of sugar, salt, and oil, but few vitamins or minerals. Your body becomes weak and gains extra weight. You get tired, your teeth decay, and your energy drops.'

points.text: Junk food fills you up but doesn't nourish you.
Too much junk food leads to health problems.

slides.title: Reading Food Labels
slides.storyContext: Doctor Priya teaches Ravi to read packages and understand what he's eating.

points.label: Ingredients list
points.text: Listed by weight. First ingredient is most abundant. Shorter lists are often healthier.

points.label: Nutrition facts
points.text: Shows calories, protein, carbs, fat, sodium, sugar per serving. Lower sugar and sodium are better.

points.label: Expiry date
points.text: Never eat expired food. Check it's fresh and safe.

slides.inSimpleWords: Food labels tell you exactly what's inside so you can make smart choices.

points.text: Smart eating starts with reading what's on the package.

slides.title: Comparing Two Cereals
slides.storyContext: Ravi compares two breakfast cereals at the store.

example.problem: Cereal A: 30g sugar per 100g, lots of additives, bright colors. Cereal B: 5g sugar per 100g, whole grains listed first, few additives. Which is healthier?
example.solution: Cereal B is much healthier. It has way less sugar (5g vs 30g) and whole grains provide energy without the crash. Cereal A is basically candy disguised as breakfast.

points.text: Lower sugar = better for energy and health.
Whole grains are real food, not processed.

slides.title: Ravi's Two-Month Journey
slides.storyContext: After 2 months of balanced eating, water, and exercise, Ravi returns to Doctor Priya. 'I can run faster! I scored better in math tests! My skin is clearer!' Doctor Priya smiles. 'That's nutrition and hydration working together. Your brain got better nutrients, your body got fuel and water. Everything improved!'

points.text: Good nutrition affects your whole body and mind.
Changes happen in weeks, not days—be patient and consistent.

slides.title: Digestion - From Mouth to Stomach
slides.storyContext: Doctor Priya explains the journey food takes inside your body.

points.label: Mouth
points.text: Teeth chew food into small pieces. Saliva starts breaking it down.

points.label: Stomach
points.text: Mixes food with acid and churns it into a paste for 2-4 hours.

points.label: Small intestine
points.text: Absorbs all nutrients into your blood. Takes 6+ hours.

points.label: Large intestine
points.text: Takes remaining water. Waste becomes stool.

slides.inSimpleWords: Your body breaks down food into tiny parts so it can absorb the good stuff.

points.text: Digestion is a complex process that takes hours.

slides.title: Why We Chew Our Food
slides.storyContext: Ravi asks why his mummy always says 'chew properly.'

example.problem: Ravi gulps his food in 2 minutes vs chewing it slowly for 20 minutes. Which is better and why?
example.solution: Slow chewing is much better. Chewing breaks food into tiny pieces (bigger surface area), saliva mixes in (starts digestion), and slow eating gives your brain time to signal 'full.' Result: better digestion, more nutrients absorbed, less likely to overeat.

points.text: Proper chewing = better digestion and nutrition.
Eating slowly = eating smarter.

slides.title: Food Choices Everywhere
slides.storyContext: Ravi notices food choices in his daily life: school tiffin, restaurant menus, snack shops, birthday parties. 'Now I understand every food choice has consequences,' he thinks. 'I can pick samosa or salad. Chocolate or apple. Soda or water. Each choice affects my energy and health.' He feels empowered—he's not just eating, he's making smart decisions.

points.text: Every food choice matters, even small ones.
Knowledge gives you power to choose better.

slides.title: Ravi Teaches His Parents
slides.storyContext: Ravi comes home excited. He teaches his parents everything: the food groups, why vitamins matter, how to read labels. His mummy laughs. 'My son is now the food expert in this house!' Soon the whole family is eating balanced meals and drinking more water.

points.text: Healthy habits spread through families.
Knowledge shared is power shared.

slides.title: Ravi's Health Promise
slides.storyContext: Ravi feels stronger now. He tells Doctor Priya his plan to stay healthy.

points.text: Eat foods from all groups: grains, protein, vegetables, fruits, and dairy.
Eat different colored foods to get all vitamins and minerals.
Drink plenty of clean water every day.
Wash hands and keep food clean.
Eat healthy to run faster, think better, and stay strong.

slides.inSimpleWords: Eating right makes you healthy, strong, smart, and happy.

image.alt: Ravi's Health Promise — Food and Health
